newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-European air fares rise as fuel prices jump.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-European air fares rise as fuel prices jump.

text.p: The highest fuel costs for six years have forced British Airways Plc to raise European airfares and other carriers may be forced to follow, industry sources said on Wednesday.

BA, one of the world's largest airlines, said it was increasing full, published fares on its European routes by 2.5 percent on average from the middle of October and considering increases for long-haul destinations.
"We have been forced to file a number of fare increases recently, primarily as a result of the leaping cost of aviation fuel," a spokesman told Reuters.
Belgian national airline Sabena said it would raise the full fare for its flights to London and Manchester from Brussels by 2.5 percent in response.
Other European carriers were also considering fare rises.
"A definitive decision can be expected shortly," KLM Royal Dutch Airlines spokesman Peter Wellhuner said.

Wellhuner said KLM was smarting from the increase in fuel prices, up by about 30 percent since mid-July as Middle East tension, low stocks and strong demand combined to propel world oil markets to levels not seen since the 1990-1991 Iraq crisis.
KLM's charter units Transavia and Martinair said on Tuesday they were introducing a fuel surcharge on winter bookings for departures from November 1 until March 31.

Virgin Atlantic, British Midland, Finnair, and Austrian Airlines, however, said long-term supply contracts and hedging strategies -- buying fuel in advance -- had given them enough protection to ride out the turbulence.
But if current prices persist, few were expected to escape the cost squeeze unscathed, industry sources said.
"In the longer term it will have some impact on fares," said Virgin Atlantic's corporate communications manager Tracy Meaker.

Analysts said the oil rally shows no sign of ending soon and prices could leap again if last winter's frigid temperatures are repeated, leaving consumers scrambling for scarce heating oil in Europe and the United States.
"Any oil consumer will be very, very vulnerable to a cold winter," said a jet trader for a Wall Street bank.
"Airlines anticipated a big move down earlier this year and they have been caught licking their wounds," he added.
Even the most sophisticated hedging strategy could be blown away, dealers said.
"Some will have hedged the risk but many will not have anticipated the price would be where it is -- painfully high," said a jet buyer at a major European airline.
European jet fuel was trading at about $266 a tonne on Wednesday, up from $200 on July 15 and nearly $100 above 1995's spot market average.
The outlook for airlines and their customers was little better, traders said. Jet fuel for delivery in the first three months of 1997 was priced at $246 a tonne on Wednesday.
Any extension of the rally into the second quarter of 1997 could hit the price of next summer's package holidays.

The Association of British Travel Agents (ABTA), which represents 620 British tour operators and 7,000 travel agents, said it had not yet received any requests to authorise surcharges to brochure prices published in recent weeks.
"There's has been not one request so far but we have been expecting them," said an ABTA spokeswoman.
